Put the provincial administration on a firmer footing.
Two Crowns, One Kingdom

Ferdinand II inherits the throne in a kingdom joined under one crown but divided by geography and political memory. Naples is the seat of royal administration, while Sicily retains a strong sense of its separate institutions and grievances. The new reign has room for practical improvements: orderly accounts, reliable roads and better schools can give royal government firmer foundations. Yet public works alone will not settle the relationship between the court, provincial elites and those seeking a constitution. Ministers must build confidence before the next crisis tests the bonds between the mainland and the island.
Reconcile the Provincial Accounts
Provincial receipts arrive in Naples through uneven records and disputed exemptions. A royal commission can reconcile the ledgers, inspect collectors and establish reliable public accounts.
Repair the Roads of the Mezzogiorno
Damaged bridges and difficult roads isolate inland markets from the coast. Provincial works will repair these routes and make journeys easier for farmers, merchants and royal officials.
Fund physicians, relief kitchens and clear public notices.
Enforce cordons with the resources already available.
Cholera in the Two Sicilies

The epidemic has reached Naples and Sicily. Fear of contagion mixes with rumours of poisoning and resentment of official interference. Medical relief and reliable information cost money, but treating every frightened crowd as a conspiracy risks further unrest.
Grant the concession, despite the merchants' objections.
Keep the export trade open.
A Monopoly for Sicilian Sulphur?

Sicilian sulphur supplies an important export trade, and the French firm Taix and Aycard now offers to organise sales through an exclusive concession. Supporters argue that controlled exports could improve returns and give the crown a firmer hand over the industry. British merchants object that the monopoly threatens their commercial rights and restricts access to a valuable commodity. Granting it promises a temporary advantage in the mining districts, but risks a diplomatic quarrel with London. Keeping exports open avoids that confrontation. The concession belongs to a private firm: it is not a transfer of Sicilian territory to France.
Pay compensation and restore open exports.
Ask Paris to mediate a compensated settlement.
Maintain the concession for now.
Britain Challenges the Sulphur Concession

London's objections to the sulphur monopoly have become a confrontation over commercial rights. British naval pressure makes an extended dispute costly for a kingdom dependent on maritime exchange. The court must weigh the concession's mining advantage against the damage to commerce and its relations abroad. Compensated repeal would restore open exports, but the treasury must meet the bill. Paris may provide a channel for negotiation, although French mediation cannot be assumed. Maintaining the concession postpones the expense and leaves the commercial penalty in place until ministers can arrange a settlement.
Offer a channel for a compensated settlement.
Decline to take responsibility for the dispute.
Mediation between London and Naples

The Neapolitan government asks us to help resolve the sulphur dispute. Mediation would protect French commercial interests without treating the private concession as a national territorial claim. Naples must still compensate the firm if it accepts a settlement.
Accept the settlement and compensate the concessionaires.
We cannot complete this settlement now.
A French Channel for Settlement

Paris will assist negotiations, but assistance does not erase the kingdom's contractual obligations. The crown can now unwind the concession with compensation and a smaller diplomatic loss. If the treasury cannot meet the cost, the dispute will remain open.
Prepare to settle directly with the merchants.
Paris Declines Mediation
France will not undertake the requested mediation. The sulphur concession remains our responsibility. A direct compensated settlement is still available through the royal government.
Settle the Sulphur Dispute
The sulphur concession has strained commerce and relations with Britain. Ministers propose compensating the concessionaires and reopening exports to bring the dispute to an end.
Build the Napoli-Portici Railway
A railway along the bay will connect Naples with Portici and the royal residences. Its opening will demonstrate the possibilities of steam transport to engineers, merchants and the court.
A beginning for the royal railways.
The Railway to Portici

The new line carries the royal party from Naples towards Portici. Its length is modest, but the spectacle of steam traction gives the kingdom a visible place in the railway age. Maintaining and extending the line will demand engineers, machinery and sustained investment.
Establish the Pietrarsa Workshops
Imported machinery leaves the royal railway dependent on foreign repair crews. Workshops at Pietrarsa will train mechanics and develop the kingdom's own engineering experience.
Found the Vesuvius Observatory

Vesuvius dominates the bay, but scattered accounts cannot replace systematic observation. A permanent observatory will provide instruments, trained observers and a continuing record of the volcano's behaviour.
Welcome the scientists and publish their observations.
Science beneath Vesuvius

Naples hosts the seventh Congress of Italian Scientists in the autumn of 1845. Royal patronage gives the gathering public standing, while officials remain wary of the political connections among its visitors. Scientific exchange brings prestige and research experience. A funded Vesuvius Observatory can contribute further observations under Macedonio Melloni, but the congress does not depend on the player having built it. The gathering encourages communication across Italian states without imposing a national government or a constitutional reform.
Fund Parish and Municipal School Grants
Parish and municipal schools lack consistent support beyond the capital. Grants for instructors, books and schoolrooms will help the kingdom train the clerks, artisans and teachers it needs.
Negotiate Commerce with the United States
Atlantic commerce needs a dependable diplomatic framework. A mission to Washington will seek commercial and navigation rights, although American ministers must decide whether to accept our proposals.
Approve the commercial agreement.
Decline the proposal.
A Commercial Treaty with Naples
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies proposes reciprocal recognition of commercial and navigation rights. Accepting will improve diplomatic relations without committing us to defend the Bourbon crown.
Ratify the agreement.
Commerce across the Atlantic

The American government has accepted our commercial agreement. Neapolitan and Sicilian merchants gain a clearer diplomatic framework for trade. The treaty is a commercial settlement, not an American guarantee of the dynasty.
Close the mission's accounts.
The American Mission Returns

The American government has declined the proposal, or circumstances no longer permit its completion. The mission returns half of its reserved negotiating funds. The cost of dispatching it is not recovered.
Investigate grievances while restoring order.
Restore order through the royal authorities.
Unrest in Calabria and Messina

Insurrectionary attempts in Calabria and Messina expose the distance between court proclamations and provincial loyalties. The immediate disturbances can be contained, but demands for constitutional government and Sicilian autonomy remain unresolved.
Promise a constitution and instruct the ministers to prepare it.
Retain the existing government and confront the revolt.
The January Crisis of 1848

The revolt at Palermo in January 1848 confronts the Bourbon government with a constitutional and Sicilian crisis. Agitation is spreading to the mainland, and concessions can no longer be treated as a distant administrative question. The king may promise a charter, but its promulgation will follow in February rather than taking effect immediately. This promise does not concede Sicilian independence or cancel the native revolution. The court still has to decide how to translate its pledge into government.
Dissolve the constitutional experiment.
Keep the charter and dismiss the hardliners.
The Barricades of Naples

The constitutional experiment has brought deputies to Naples without resolving their relationship with the crown. Disagreement over the parliamentary oath and the limits of royal authority has moved from debate to barricades. Soldiers and armed opponents now face one another in the capital. On 15 May 1848, the historical confrontation ended in a royal victory and the destruction of the experiment. Ministers must decide whether to dissolve the new political order or defend the charter against the court's hardliners. Restoring absolute rule will deepen popular resentment, while preserving the charter risks alienating reactionary supporters.
Offer administrative amnesties and rebuild the districts.
Reassert royal authority without new expenditure.
Royal Government Returns to Sicily

The crown once again holds Palermo, Messina and Catania, and an independent Sicilian government no longer stands against it. Military success has restored royal administration, but the campaign has left damaged livelihoods and bitter memories. Ministers can combine reconstruction with administrative amnesties, hoping that restraint will make the return of royal government more durable. Such a programme requires money, and its benefits will take time to reach the districts. A punitive settlement avoids immediate expenditure and satisfies those who demand obedience, but risks turning the island's defeat into a continuing source of resentment.
Authorize inspections and review political cases.
Reject the accusations as interference.
Gladstone and the Political Prisons

William Gladstone's accounts of political imprisonment in Naples are circulating abroad. His accusations have found an audience in Britain, where the treatment of prisoners is becoming a question of Bourbon legitimacy as well as prison administration. The court regards the criticism as an attack on its sovereignty, but denunciations alone cannot restore confidence. Inspections and reviews of political cases would require staff, funding and a willingness to examine the conduct of royal officials. Refusing the criticism preserves an uncompromising position while further damaging relations with Britain and drawing public attention to the controversy.
Release funds for medical and municipal relief.
Rely on the existing authorities.
Another Cholera Emergency

Cholera has returned to Naples. The authorities face the practical work of relief, sanitation and public information. A funded emergency response eases the disruption. Leaving the work entirely to existing institutions avoids a new bill but increases public anger.
Offer a limited amnesty and reopen diplomatic channels.
Refuse the foreign demands.
The Diplomatic Isolation of 1856

British and French pressure over Bourbon government has deepened after the Crimean War and the Paris settlement. The court sees reform demands as interference. A limited amnesty may ease tensions, while an uncompromising reply strengthens royal hardliners and leaves the kingdom more isolated.
Fund a provincial inquiry and local relief.
Treat the expedition as a warning to strengthen vigilance.
Pisacane's Expedition to Sapri

Carlo Pisacane's expedition has landed near Sapri in June 1857 after freeing prisoners on Ponza. It hopes to turn revolutionary theory into a southern uprising, but distrust and local opposition frustrate the enterprise. The crown must address the provincial grievances that made such a gamble possible.
Maintain the royal administration under the new king.
Francis II Inherits the Crown

Ferdinand II died at Caserta on 22 May 1859, leaving the throne to Francis II. The new king inherits a substantial royal administration and armed forces, but also the distrust accumulated through constitutional conflict, Sicilian resistance and diplomatic isolation. At the same time, events elsewhere in Italy are changing the balance on which the Bourbon kingdom has relied. An inexperienced court must learn to coordinate ministers and commanders while deciding which inherited policies to preserve. The transition temporarily weakens army organisation, making preparation and reliable supply more urgent as the new reign begins.
Organise Defence of the Straits
The narrow sea between Sicily and Calabria has become a military frontier. Patrols, signals and reliable provisioning will help naval commanders coordinate the defence of both shores.
Reorganise the Bourbon Army Supply Board
Loyalty alone cannot keep regiments supplied in the field. A central board will review stores, transport contracts and equipment accounts before the next emergency tests the royal army.
Restore constitutional government.
Keep the existing royal government.
A Last Constitutional Opening

The danger to the kingdom has made another constitutional opening urgent. The court needs support beyond its traditional loyalists, while liberals doubt that promises will survive once the immediate threat has passed. In June 1860, Francis II historically restored constitutional government in an effort to widen the monarchy's base. A new charter may ease liberal resentment and give ministers a different political footing, but it will also anger royal hardliners. It cannot recall an expedition already under way or end an existing war. The crown must decide whether the risks of reform now outweigh those of continued intransigence.
Provision the Fortress of Gaeta
With Naples occupied, Gaeta shelters the remaining Bourbon forces. Provisions, maintenance crews and repaired defences will help the fortress withstand the approaching siege.
Close the mission and recover the reserve.
The Commercial Negotiations Lapse
The disappearance of the proposed treaty partner has ended the negotiations. The mission returns its unused reserve, while its dispatch costs remain spent.
Return the dispute to our own ministers.
The Mediation Channel Closes
The requested French mediation can no longer proceed. The concession remains unresolved, and the crown must arrange a direct settlement.

Lay a Development Programme Before the Crown

The crown must decide how to develop the kingdom. Countryside improvement, royal industry and balanced renewal offer different opportunities, while selective projects preserve greater freedom for the court.
Retain selective royal projects.
Give priority to the countryside.
Seek greater industrial independence.
Renew the provincial administration.
What Kind of Kingdom Shall We Build?

Petitions from the provinces lie beside the accounts of the royal works. Landowners ask for roads and clearer titles, merchants for credit, and the officers at Pietrarsa for trained hands and dependable orders. His Majesty cannot grant every request. One body of ministers would begin with the countryside, another would make the workshops instruments of royal strength, while a third urges schools and provincial offices before grand undertakings. Each proposal has its advocates at court and its opponents beyond Naples. The council must settle which enterprises shall receive the crown's continuing attention, or leave the ministries to pursue their separate projects.
Survey Titles and Communal Rights
Surveyors will compare land titles, village boundaries and disputed rights of use. A reliable register can clarify public accounts, but established proprietors will resist scrutiny of their claims.
Audit the Village Grain Funds

Village grain funds should lend seed when households need it and recover stocks after harvest. Published accounts and inspected stores will help protect rural families from dependence on private lenders.
Convene Tribunals on the Commons

The surveys expose overlapping private titles and communal claims. Provincial tribunals must decide whether to uphold existing deeds, protect village rights of use or establish smallholdings on disputed public land.
Uphold the established deeds.
Protect documented village rights of use.
Create smallholdings and review their survival.
Whose Land Is the Common?

The commissioners have received deeds bearing proper seals, petitions bearing the names of entire villages, and testimony that agrees upon scarcely a boundary. A proprietor insists that the court protect his title. The villagers answer that their fathers cut wood and grazed animals upon the same ground without asking his leave. Upholding the deeds would satisfy the owners, while preserving customary access would sustain the villages. Dividing disputed public land into smallholdings offers another settlement, but possession alone will not furnish a poor household with seed, animals or credit. Whatever judgment is issued, the provincial authorities must enforce it among neighbours who will continue to live beside one another.
The grain funds have sustained the new proprietors.
Record the losses and the growing resentment.
The old commission no longer has jurisdiction.
Two Harvests After the Settlement

The first deeds are now two harvests old. Where grain funds kept seed within reach, the new households have a firmer footing. Elsewhere, creditors are gathering the plots back together. The registers record a real change only if the families can continue working the land.
Endow Provincial Discount Offices

Merchants beyond the capital need dependable access to commercial credit. Supervised provincial offices can support their trade, but troubled loans and reserve obligations will require continuing attention from the treasury.
Provide an audited reserve.
Let the offices contract their lending.
Close the old commission.
The First Provincial Credit Examination

The provincial offices have begun to send their accounts to Naples. Among the merchants' bills are overdue advances, disputed securities and promises resting upon a harvest yet to be gathered. The inspectors believe the offices can continue if the treasury provides a reserve and requires their books to be published. Others at the council fear that an advance today will become an expectation tomorrow. Refusing assistance preserves the treasury's resources, but sound merchants may suffer alongside doubtful borrowers when credit contracts. The ministry must decide how much confidence it will place in these new provincial institutions.
Support the Bari office.
Postpone the appropriation.
A Provincial Bank Office at Bari

A bank office at Bari offers a practical extension of the kingdom's financial administration beyond Naples. An appropriation can provide premises, staff and working funds. The concession remains limited: a single office does not yet supply the whole mainland with credit. Ministers must decide whether the treasury can carry the expense.
Train Mechanics for Pietrarsa

Buying machines cannot replace technical knowledge. Apprenticeships, drawing instruction and maintenance practice around Pietrarsa will develop skilled workers, who may also demand a greater voice in public life.
Place Supply Contracts at Mongiana
Regular orders and inspected deliveries can connect the Calabrian works more closely with the royal army. Accountable contracts will strengthen the supply of tools, stores and military equipment.
Modernise the Castellammare Workshops
Steam machinery demands repair skills, fuel stores and dependable naval accounts. Workshops at Castellammare will help the existing fleet meet these demands and maintain its readiness at sea.
Institute Provincial Administrative Examinations

Provincial renewal needs trained officials and teachers. Examinations and common record forms will improve their work, while challenging the patronage through which many appointments have traditionally been made.
Negotiate a Settlement with Palermo

A royal commission can negotiate with Palermo while the island remains under the crown. Provincial consultation or a separate parliament may ease resentment, but concessions will limit Naples's control over island affairs.
Preserve the common royal administration.
Guarantee consultation and a published island budget.
Restore an island parliament under the common crown.
The Institutions of the Island

Palermo's delegates have come with petitions concerning the island's revenues and the officials sent to administer them. They ask who may approve expenditure in Sicily and who shall answer when the accounts are disputed. The ministers offer a consultative council through which the island may be heard without recovering a legislature. The stronger proposal would establish an island parliament and a separate budget, binding the crown to a more considerable bargain. Neither side has forgotten the troops and proclamations of earlier confrontations. A settlement signed at the conference must also command confidence in the towns where it will be put into practice.
The guarantees have lost their authority.
The Palermo Settlement Under Strain

The institutions agreed with Palermo have failed to contain a renewed crisis. Armed defiance and extraordinary public anger have undermined the agreement. The crown can no longer treat the island as reconciled merely because a charter was once signed. Existing grievances and the ordinary revolutionary struggle will decide what follows.
Review the Promotion of Royal Officers

A commission will examine promotion, staff training and the obligations of command. Professional standards promise a more capable army, while unsettling courtiers who regard personal loyalty as the foundation of service.
Keep royal confidence at the centre of promotion.
Adopt examinations and professional staff training.
Loyalty and Professional Command

The commission has found that discipline and expertise are different questions. The crown can preserve a system of personal confidence, or bind advancement more closely to examinations and staff practice. Professional standards improve coordination, but they also give officers a corporate voice which the court cannot always control.
Maintain the inherited system.
Grant a conservative constitution and review political cases.
Filangieri and the New Reign

The accession of Francis has brought a new round of audiences, memorials and urgent advice. Filangieri counsels the young king to gather support before the kingdom's enemies can profit from its divisions. A conservative constitution might draw men of property and moderate opinion back towards the throne and furnish the diplomats with a stronger case abroad. At court, the defenders of the inherited order warn that a concession made under pressure will invite further demands. The king must judge whether reform can preserve the authority of his house, or whether the old system can still command the obedience upon which that authority rests.
Seek a French Understanding
Constitutional reform offers our diplomats an opening in Paris. A mission can seek renewed consultation, though French cooperation will depend on its own ambitions and interests in Italy.
Decline a new commitment.
Receive the mission and exchange assurances.
An Opening from Naples

The constitutional government in Naples proposes diplomatic consultation. Its envoys hope to reduce the kingdom's isolation, but our Italian commitments may point in another direction. Receiving the mission would improve relations without promising intervention or changing the independence of either state.
Enter the answer in the diplomatic record.
The Mission Is Received

Paris has accepted diplomatic consultation. Relations have improved, but the assurances contain no military guarantee. The kingdom must still maintain its own defences and make its institutions credible.
Enter the answer in the diplomatic record.
Paris Declines the Opening

The French government has declined a new understanding. The mission has spent its appropriation without obtaining a commitment. Reform at home must stand on its own merits, and the kingdom remains responsible for its own defence.
Consolidate the Rural Programme

The countryside programme has established registers, village credit and rural institutions. Their continuing administration can consolidate agricultural renewal, though the crown must still balance rural needs against industrial ambitions.
Consolidate the Workshop Programme

The industrial programme has developed workshops, technical instruction and supply contracts. Consolidating these institutions will strengthen manufacturing while binding the treasury to their continuing support.
Consolidate the Renewal Programme

Schools, provincial administration and selective investment have given renewal a broad foundation. Sustaining these institutions will help the kingdom develop without committing every resource to a single sector.
Publish the accounts and continue the work.
A Programme Becomes an Institution

What began as separate petitions and royal authorisations now has offices, trained servants and accounts of its own. Provincial officials know where to send their returns, and the establishments can expect continuing attention rather than await another favour from court. The council has approved the means to sustain the institutions raised under the chosen programme. Their reputation will depend upon the conduct of the men appointed to them: a school needs instructors, a credit office careful clerks, and a workshop orders that arrive before its skilled hands depart. The crown has acquired a more enduring instrument of government, together with the obligation to keep it in good order.
Reopen the civil accounts and recognise the work of reconstruction.
The Kingdom Beyond the Crisis

The kingdom has survived the years in which its independence was most threatened. Peace gives the government a chance to assess the institutions it preserved and the concessions it made. Survival does not settle the Italian question, nor does it erase provincial grievances. The councils must now turn emergency measures into a workable ordinary administration.
Extend the Railway Programme to Bari
A railway towards Bari would connect the Adriatic provinces with the capital. Engineers must survey the route and organise construction before the promised commercial advantages can be realised.
Open the completed section.
Close the commission without a new line.

Finance the Calabrian Railway Section

Debate the Crown and the Italian Nation

The kingdom's development has raised a larger question: what role should Naples play in Italy? Ministers must choose between a federal crown, centralized constitutional leadership, an absolute national monarchy or continued restraint.
Retain the southern kingdom's present commitments.
Build a centralized constitutional kingdom under Naples.
Entrust national leadership to an undivided absolute crown.
The Crown and the Nation

Development has strengthened parts of the kingdom without deciding who may govern it. A federal crown would protect the Palermo compact and negotiate wider Italian cooperation. A centralized constitutional kingdom would place representative government and national administration under Naples. An absolute crown would claim the same leadership while refusing parliamentary restraint. These are exclusive political mandates. The southern status quo remains available, but adopting a new mandate commits the court to its institutions, opposition and future Italian policy.
Propose an Italian League at Rome
An alliance with the Papal government could bring independent Italian crowns into closer consultation. Rome may welcome the proposal or refuse it, preserving its freedom to pursue a different policy.
Decline the proposed league.
Conclude the alliance while preserving Papal sovereignty.
A League of Italian Crowns?

Naples proposes an alliance under a common Italian understanding. The proposal leaves Papal sovereignty intact, but even a limited league might involve Rome in rivalries between Naples, Turin and Vienna. The government must judge the offer for itself. Refusal closes this mission without preventing later ordinary diplomacy.
Receive the delegation's report.
The Roman Articles Are Signed

Rome has accepted the alliance. The Papal government remains sovereign, and Naples has gained a diplomatic partner rather than an Italian crown. The league must now survive the competing ambitions and obligations of its members.
Receive the delegation's report.
Rome Declines the League

The Papal government has declined the proposed alliance. The delegation returns with no treaty. The crown must pursue its Italian ambitions through other partners, or reconsider the obligations it is prepared to undertake.

Ferdinand II and the Cost of the Court

The accession of Ferdinand II in November 1830 has raised expectations at Naples. The young king reduces expenditure at court, replaces ministers and extends clemency to some political prisoners. Officers associated with the Murat period can return to royal service. These measures seek a stronger Bourbon administration, not parliamentary government. The crown remains absolute, and the relationship between Naples and Sicily will test how far administrative renewal can resolve political grievances.
Recognise the convention and open regular diplomatic channels.
The American Claims Convention

Formal diplomatic relations with the United States began in January 1832. A convention signed that October addresses American claims arising from seizures during the Murat era. Recognition and the settlement belong together: compensation repairs an inherited dispute, while resident diplomatic representatives establish a channel for later commercial negotiations. This agreement does not itself confer free trade or the privileges of the separate 1845 treaty.
Discharge the American Claims Settlement
Claims arising from Murat-era seizures still burden relations with Washington. Compensation and a settlement of outstanding accounts will clear the way for later commercial negotiations.
Organise the Internal Security Guard

Royal policing depends on coordination between the capital and provincial authorities. An internal security formation can strengthen public order, while giving officials a more prominent role in local affairs.

Instruct officials to explain quarantine and hear grievances.
Poison Rumours and the Sicilian Cholera Revolts

Cholera has spread through the kingdom, and rumours in Sicily accuse the authorities of poisoning the population. In the summer of 1837 unrest in Syracuse and Catania turned disease and distrust into a political crisis. Royal commissioners answered with repression. The island districts now face both an epidemic and hostility toward Naples. A military response may restore immediate order, but its consequences will outlast the emergency and deepen the resentment of royal administration.

Feudal abolition left disputes over dues, compensation and communal rights. District reviews can settle these accounts, easing rural grievances while challenging inherited privileges.
Coordinate the Railway to Caserta
The railway now reaches inland towards Cancello and Caserta. Connecting roads, freight arrangements and an organised terminus will help neighbouring districts share in its commercial advantages.
Carry out the sentences of the military tribunal.

The Bandiera Expedition

Attilio and Emilio Bandiera have landed in Calabria with companions who expect a popular rising against Bourbon rule. Their venture fails to gather the support they anticipated, and the authorities capture the party. A military trial at Cosenza condemns its leaders. Nine participants, including the brothers, were executed on 25 July 1844. Their deaths will become a symbol for Italian nationalists, even though the expedition itself has failed to overturn royal government.
